questions.q: According to the Architect's Code of Ethical Conduct, what is the architect's moral responsibility regarding the project's budget?
o: To reimburse the owner for any amount exceeding the original budget
To provide the client with a realistic estimate of cost and not to guarantee the cost of the work
To guarantee that the final construction cost will match the initial bid
To ensure the project is completed at the lowest possible cost regardless of quality
questions.n: The architect's duty is to provide professional estimates based on current data without making a legal guarantee of the final price.

questions.q: Is an architect allowed to accept 'free' technical services or commissions from manufacturers or suppliers of building materials?
o: Yes, as long as the client is informed
No, this is a conflict of interest and a violation of Integrity and Independence
Only if the value of the service is below Php 50,000
Yes, if the services are related to sustainable or 'green' products
questions.n: Accepting such favors can bias the architect's specifications, violating their duty to provide objective professional advice.

questions.q: What must an architect do if a client asks them to take over a project that is already being handled by another architect?
o: Begin work immediately to ensure the client's needs are met
Ensure the previous architect's services have been officially terminated and financial obligations settled
Offer a lower fee than the previous architect to secure the contract
Request a copy of the previous architect's drawings to use as a base
questions.n: Ethics require a clean 'hand-off' to protect the previous architect's right to compensation and intellectual property.

questions.q: Under the 'Ethics to the Public,' what is the architect’s primary duty in terms of the environment?
o: To minimize construction time to reduce local noise pollution
To follow the owner's instructions even if they violate environmental laws
To always use the most expensive materials to ensure building longevity
To promote sustainable development and protect public health, safety, and welfare
questions.n: Architects are stewards of the built environment and must consider the long-term impact of their designs on the ecosystem.

questions.q: Can an architect use 'competitive bidding' or 'under-cutting' of fees to win a project?
o: No, this is considered unprofessional and unethical behavior among colleagues
Yes, it is a standard practice in a free-market economy
Only if the project is for a non-profit organization
Yes, provided the fee does not drop below 2% of construction cost
questions.n: Professional fees are based on the value of service; under-cutting devalues the profession and leads to poor service quality.

questions.q: What type of buildings fall under Group 1 (Simplest Structures), such as Armories and Hangars?
o: Structures with exceptional interior details
Simplest Structures with a BPF usually starting at 5% of project cost
Structures with a BPF starting at 10%
Residential condominiums and office buildings
questions.n: Group 1 buildings have large open spaces and repetitive elements, requiring less intensive architectural detail.

questions.q: Group 2 involves structures of moderate complexity. Which building types are classified here?
o: Laboratories and Theaters
Residential Condominiums, Office Buildings, Art Galleries, and Schools
Monuments and Mausoleums
Bakeries and Freight Depots
questions.n: These buildings require more detailed planning for utilities, partitions, and circulation than Group 1.

questions.q: Which group covers buildings with exceptional architectural character, such as Aquariums and Laboratories?
o: Group 3 (Structures of Exceptional Complexity)
Group 6
Group 2
Group 1
questions.n: These buildings require highly specialized knowledge of systems, life support, or acoustics.

questions.q: What is the typical BPF percentage for a Group 2 project with a construction cost of Php 50 Million or less?
o: 6% of the Project Construction Cost
questions.n: Under SPP Doc 202, Group 2 structures start with a 6% fee for the first 50M of cost.

questions.q: If a client builds several 'repetitive' houses using the same plans, how is the BPF for the succeeding units calculated?
o: Full BPF is charged for every unit
The architect is only paid for the first unit
A fixed fee of Php 10,000 per unit
Decreasing Percentages (e.g., 60% for the 2nd unit, 40% for the 3rd)
questions.n: The fee is reduced for subsequent units because the architect's effort is focused on site adaptation rather than new design.

questions.q: Which method of compensation is most common for projects where the construction cost can be reasonably estimated?
o: Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses
Per Diem plus Expenses
Lump Sum
Percentage of Project Construction Cost (PPCC)
questions.n: PPCC is the most traditional method, tying the architect's fee to the scale and value of the physical project.

questions.q: What method is used for services that are non-creative or clerical in nature, or when time is the primary variable?
o: Percentage of Construction Cost
Unit Cost Method
Multiple of Direct Personnel Expenses (MDPE)
Professional Fee plus Expenses
questions.n: MDPE accounts for the actual hours spent by the architect and staff, multiplied to cover overhead.

questions.q: What is the 'Multiplier' range typically used in the MDPE method to cover overhead and profit?
questions.n: This range is the industry standard for ensuring the firm covers its technical, administrative, and profit margins.

questions.q: Which method is best for a client who needs a specific, small-scale task with a clear beginning and end?
o: Retainer
Lump Sum or Fixed Fee
MDPE
Percentage of Construction Cost
questions.n: This provides the client with a predictable cost for a clearly defined limited scope of work.

questions.q: What is 'Per Diem' compensation?
o: The final payment made upon project completion
A percentage of the project's profit
A daily allowance or fixed daily fee for work away from home base
A fee based on the number of drawings produced
questions.n: Per Diem covers the architect's time and living expenses while traveling for site visits or meetings.

questions.q: Under Section 39 of RA 9266, can a person who is not an RLA use the title 'Architectural Designer'?
o: Yes, as long as they don't sign plans
Yes, if they have a degree in architecture
No, any title conveying the impression of being an architect is prohibited
Only if they work for a construction company
questions.n: The law protects the title to prevent public confusion and ensure only licensed individuals practice.

questions.q: Is it legal for a non-architect to 'sign and seal' architectural plans even if they own the building?
o: No, only a Registered and Licensed Architect (RLA) can sign and seal
Only if they are a Civil Engineer
Yes, if the building is only one story high
Yes, owners have the right to sign their own property plans
questions.n: Only an RLA is legally and civilly liable for the architectural design under the law.

questions.q: What is the fine for any person who uses a revoked or suspended Certificate of Registration to practice architecture?
o: Php 5,000 to Php 10,000
No fine, only community service
questions.n: RA 9266 imposes heavy fines to deter the illegal practice of architecture by unlicensed or suspended persons.

questions.q: Can a foreign architect practice architecture in the Philippines without a Special Temporary Permit (STP)?
o: Yes, if they are in partnership with a Filipino architect
Yes, if they are famous internationally
No, practicing without an STP is a violation of Section 39
Only for residential projects
questions.n: Foreigners must go through the proper PRC and BoA channels to ensure reciprocity and legal standing.

questions.q: What is the role of the IAPOA (UAP) in enforcing Section 39?
o: They act as the judge and jury in criminal cases
They assist the BoA in monitoring and reporting illegal practices
They provide free legal defense for all architects
They issue the building permits directly
questions.n: The UAP helps the government by gathering data on unlicensed practitioners and ensuring only RLAs are signed on permits.

questions.q: Under SPP Doc 301, what is the 'Contract Time'?
o: The 15-day period for permit issuance
The period allowed for the completion of the work
The time spent in bidding and negotiation
The time the architect spends on drawings
questions.n: It is the agreed-upon duration for the contractor to finish the physical construction.

questions.q: What is the 'Performance Bond' required from the contractor?
o: A bond that ensures the building is earthquake-proof
A payment made to the local government for utilities
A financial guarantee that the contractor will execute the work
A guarantee that the architect will be paid
questions.n: It protects the owner if the contractor fails to perform or completes the work improperly.

questions.q: What is the definition of 'Substantial Completion'?
o: When the architect finishes the final punch list
When 50% of the building is finished
When the building permit is first issued
When the project is sufficiently complete for its intended purpose
questions.n: This is the point where the owner can start moving in or utilizing the space, usually at 95% completion.

questions.q: What is the 'Defects Liability Period' (or Maintenance Period)?
o: The duration of the construction phase
The time the architect has to finish drawings
The time allowed for the owner to pay the architect
The period during which the contractor must repair any defects
questions.n: Usually lasting one year, this ensures the contractor fixes issues like leaks or cracks after handover.

questions.q: What document does the architect issue to certify that the contractor is entitled to payment?
o: Notice to Proceed
Building Permit
Bill of Materials
Certificate of Payment
questions.n: This document validates that a specific amount of work has been done and the contractor should be paid.
